response.answer: For high-cardinality features, use embedding dimensions of 10-20 or hashing with a size of 10-20 to balance dimensionality and collision. Embeddings are preferred for better performance, while hashing is more memory-efficient.

results.title: Navigating High Cardinality: Understanding the Hashing Trick | by Steni Sebastian | Medium
results.content: I recently stumbled upon a really cool feature engineering technique on dealing categorical variable with high cardinality — ***Feature hashing***, otherwise called ***hashing trick***. Feature hashing, also known as the hashing trick, is a technique used in machine learning to encode arbitrary features into fixed size vector representations in a fast and memory-efficient manner. ### Why do we need Feature Hashing? ### Mathematical Motivation behind Feature Hashing. Instead, we can use a hash function h to randomly map words to indices:. We just use the hash index ***h(w)*** directly as the index in the feature vector, without needing to store the full mapping. There will be collisions with different words hashing to the same index:. We can use hashing to randomly assign an index to each product:. In the context of feature hashing, which is commonly used in machine learning and natural language processing, the hash size determines the number of bins or buckets into which high-cardinality categorical features are mapped. For instance, if you are applying feature hashing to convert a set of categorical features with high cardinality into a fixed number of features, the hash size would represent the number of features or “buckets” you want to map these categorical values into. Choosing an appropriate hash size is important because it impacts the dimensionality and sparsity of the resulting feature space. A larger hash size may provide more distinct buckets but can also lead to increased dimensionality, while a smaller hash size can cause collisions where multiple distinct values are mapped to the same bucket. In short, feature hashing gets around the problem of dimensionality following memory issue by using hash functions to randomly map each feature value to a numeric hash code or index. These hash codes are then used directly as indices in a vector or embedding matrix to store the feature values, without having to explicitly store a mapping from values to indices. A key advantage is that the size of the hash-based feature vectors is fixed and controllable independently of the number of input features or cardinality. Feature hashing thus provides a fast, space-efficient way of encoding categorical features for machine learning models, particularly in streaming and out-of-core learning settings.

results.content: # 4 ways to encode categorical features with high cardinality. We explore 4 methods to encode categorical variables with high cardinality: target encoding, count encoding, feature hashing and embedding. # 4 Ways to Encode Categorical Features with High Cardinality – with Python Implementation. ### Learn to apply target encoding, count encoding, feature hashing and Embedding using scikit-learn and TensorFlow. In this article, we will go through 4 popular methods to encode categorical variables with high cardinality: **(1) Target encoding, (2) Count encoding, (3) Feature hashing** and **(4) Embedding**. * Overview of each encoding method *(1) Target encoding (2) Count encoding (3) Feature hashing (4) Embedding*. ### Why do we need to encode categorical features? If a categorical feature has hundreds or thousands of categories, applying one-hot encoding would add hundreds or thousands of binary variables to the features vector. So how to to encode highly cardinal categorical features without increasing the dimensionality of feature vectors? from category_encoders.target_encoder import TargetEncoder enc = TargetEncoder(cols = categorical_features).fit(x_train, y_train) X_train_encoded = enc.transform(x_train) X_test_encoded = enc.transform(x_test). from category_encoders.count import CountEncoder enc = CountEncoder(cols = categorical_features).fit(x_train, y_train) X_train_encoded = enc.transform(x_train) X_test_encoded = enc.transform(x_test). from category_encoders.hashing import HashingEncoder enc = HashingEncoder( cols = categorical_features, n_components=20*len(categorical_features) ).fit(x_train, y_train) X_train_encoded = enc.transform(x_train) X_test_encoded = enc.transform(x_test). encoded_features = .Dense( units=size if size else encoded_features.shape[-1], activation="gelu" )(encoded_features) return (inputs=input_layers, outputs=encoded_features) def build_neural_network_model(embedding_encoder): input_layers = build_input_layers(features) embeddings = embedding_encoder(input_layers) output = .Dense(units=1, activation="sigmoid")(embeddings) model = keras.Model(inputs=input_layers, outputs=output) model.compile( optimizer=.Adam(), loss=.BinaryCrossentropy(), metrics=[.AUC()] ) return model embedding_encoder = build_embeddings(64) neural_network_model = build_neural_network_model(embedding_encoder) # Training def build_dataset(x, y): dataset = {} for feat in features: if feat in categorical_features: dataset[feat] = np.array(x[feat]).reshape(-1,1).astype(str) else: dataset[feat] = np.array(x[feat]).reshape(-1,1).astype(float) return dataset, np.array(y).reshape(-1,1) x_train, y_train = build_dataset(x_train, y_train) x_test, y_test = build_dataset(x_test, y_test) history = neural_network_model.fit(x_train, y_train, batch_size=1024, epochs=5) X_train_encoded = embedding_encoder.predict(x_train, batch_size=1024) X_test_encoded = embedding_encoder.predict(x_test, batch_size=1024).
